solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: 'Scalpel … Forceps … Forceps PLEASE, nurse!' Perhaps they're stressed

definitions.meaning: the words a surgeon speaks while operating, the talk of an operation
the key words of a statement, the ones given emphasis when it is spoken

explanation.surface: A surgeon barks for instruments, getting tetchy with the nurse in theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals on PLEASE show the stress that the second reading needs: in that order of words, that is the one leaned on.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both the crucial words of a statement and, literally, talk heard in an operating theatre.

clue.text: Not in favour of getting Poles to trade wine

indicators.note: the two poles, north and south, swap places, so the N letter is traded for an S

parts.note: being against something is being anti it

explanation.surface: A buyer, opposed in principle, lets Polish merchants deal in wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like people from Poland; here they are the compass poles N and S, and the N in ANTI becomes S.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is a sparkling Italian white from Piedmont, so it is an example of a wine.

clue.text: Down with outer garments!

definitions.meaning: the French cry of protest against a person or regime
the plural of a loose sleeveless cloak worn by Arabs

explanation.surface: A rallying cry to strip off coats and jackets.
explanation.walkthrough: An aba is a loose woollen robe worn in the Arab world, so its plural fits the second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The French protest slogan is used in English too, and also spells the plural of a Middle Eastern robe.

clue.text: Evidence of Gangnam-style RTA? Examine the body

definitions.note: the noun can also be used as a verb meaning to carry out a post-mortem

parts.note: a road traffic accident involves a car, which is an auto
Psy is the Korean singer who had the hit Gangnam Style

explanation.surface: A doctor looks over the victim of a road crash for evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer the car sits on top of PSY: the picture of the singer run over, the 'evidence' of a Gangnam-style road traffic accident (RTA).
explanation.definitionFit: A post-mortem examination of a corpse; the word also serves as a verb for performing one.

clue.text: The original Biblical item? Give credit to those going to Bow Church

definitions.meaning: the first couple in Genesis, the earliest item or pairing in the Bible

definitions.text: Give credit to those going to Bow Church
definitions.meaning: to believe, as said in Cockney rhyming slang; Cockneys are born within sound of the bells of St Mary-le-Bow

explanation.surface: A church notice crediting the first Bible story to the Bow congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhyming slang is a London Cockney code where a phrase stands for the word it rhymes with; here the couple's names rhyme with 'believe'.
explanation.definitionFit: The first man and woman in Genesis, and the rhyming slang for believe, which is giving credit to something.

clue.text: Not one to move around picture frames, I gather

indicators.note: a frame goes round a picture, so the first word surrounds the next part

parts.note: a picture made with pencil is a drawing

indicators.note: the Roman numeral for one, I, is taken away

parts.note: to stir is to move something round and round

explanation.surface: Someone lazy refuses to shift the picture frames, they suppose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not one' removes I from STIR, leaving STR, which DRAWING 'frames'. 'I gather' looks like 'I suppose'; it is the cord speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A cord threaded through a hem that, when pulled, gathers the material together, so it could say this of itself.

clue.text: Try to extend Telegraph employees in pub (tied house)

indicators.note: the employees are placed inside the pub abbreviation

parts.note: PH is the abbreviation for public house
the Telegraph's own staff, writing in their own paper, call themselves us
bound means tied up
Aries is one of the twelve houses of the zodiac in astrology

explanation.surface: Newspaper staff drinking in a brewery-owned pub try to stay later.
explanation.walkthrough: A tied house is a British pub owned by a brewery and bound to sell its beer; here the bracketed phrase splits into two separate pieces, the second an astrological house.
explanation.definitionFit: To go beyond accepted limits is an idiom for attempting to enlarge what is possible.

clue.text: Stupidly they meet agent, carrying a threat ever closer

indicators.note: the jumbled letters carry, or hold, the next letter within them
acting stupidly suggests the letters are muddled into a new order

explanation.surface: Foolish spies rendezvous with an agent while a danger draws near.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stupidly' rearranges THEY MEET AGENT, and 'carrying' puts A among those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom, also a war film title, for a foe drawing near to the city, a danger approaching.

clue.text: B___ awful weather? Fancy, out of nowhere!

parts.note: the blank stands for a swear word, bloody, of which only its opening letter B is shown
a heavy downpour with wind is a rainstorm

explanation.surface: Someone curses the dreadful weather, then has a sudden whim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'B___ awful' reads as 'bloody awful', but the letter B and the weather split differently.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden bright idea that arrives unbidden is a brainwave; in American English this word means the same.

clue.text: In or out of Union, a Eurosceptic's not Scottish

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A Scottish Eurosceptic says no to the union, whether in or out.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scots word sits within unioN A Eurosceptic.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots dialect the negative is spelt this way, the equivalent of English 'no' or 'not'.

clue.text: It's said to stop mother doing her duty at 4?

definitions.text: It's said to stop mother doing her duty at 4?

parts.words: It's said to stop mother doing her duty at 4?
parts.note: at four o'clock tea-time, mother pours the tea, and a guest says this word to tell her to stop pouring

explanation.surface: A hint that something stops a mother doing her chores in the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage the person pouring tea is 'mother'; 'say ___' is what you say when your cup is full.
explanation.definitionFit: The polite word a guest utters to signal the pourer has given enough tea, ending the pouring.

clue.text: Primarily, someone suckered on the first of April

definitions.text: Primarily, someone suckered on the first of April

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the following word is taken
primarily means first of all, so the initial letters of the next two words are used

explanation.surface: Mainly, it describes a person taken in by an April Fools' Day prank.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines: an April fool is a dupe.
explanation.definitionFit: A fool or dupe, as anyone tricked on April Fools' Day becomes.

clue.text: 'Cutter' has gotten over failure to incorporate identical Ts

indicators.note: turned over, so the letters run backwards in this across answer
the word for failure takes in the next word

parts.note: a no-no is something that does not work or is not done
identical things are the same
the letter T written twice, in plural, as TS

explanation.surface: A film editor has overcome an inability to include matching Ts.
explanation.walkthrough: A no-no is a failure; 'has gotten over' turns the whole assembly backwards, and the quoted 'Cutter' is the definition, not a film editor.
explanation.definitionFit: A craftsman who shapes blocks of rock, literally a person who cuts building material.

clue.text: Being un-chirpy is typically so unfair

definitions.meaning: not being a chirping insect of the grasshopper family
an idiom for unsporting or not fair play, from the game of bat and ball

explanation.surface: Someone moaning that being glum is somehow an injustice.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket is a British bat-and-ball sport whose name became shorthand for fair play.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom says behaviour is unsporting, and read literally says something is not a chirping insect.

clue.text: Production team wrapping 007's final take of film set in the West Country

definitions.text: film set in the West Country

indicators.note: the team's letters wrap round the next part

parts.note: the people who produce something are its makers
007 is spoken double-O seven: the two Os plus the final letter of seven, N
R is the abbreviation for recipe, Latin for take, on prescriptions

explanation.surface: The crew of a Bond film shoot the last take on location in Devon or Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: Moonraker is a Bond film; the plural is a nickname for people of Wiltshire, a set of folk in England's West Country.
explanation.definitionFit: Wiltshire natives are nicknamed after a legend of yokels raking a pond for the moon, a group in south-west England.

clue.text: Cargo of pram during periods of calm?

definitions.text: Cargo of pram during periods of calm?

parts.words: Cargo of pram during periods of calm?
parts.note: a baby flings playthings out of the pram in a tantrum, so when calm they stay aboard

explanation.surface: A question about what a baby carriage holds when things are quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throwing your ___ out of the pram' is a British idiom for a tantrum.
explanation.definitionFit: Playthings carried in a baby's carriage, kept there unless a tantrum sends them overboard.

clue.text: Hand over a title once reduced by 50%

indicators.note: each word is cut to its first half

explanation.surface: A former title is handed over at half its size.
explanation.walkthrough: Halve each of 'over a title once': OV, A, TI, ON.
explanation.definitionFit: A round of applause is a hand, as in 'give them a big hand'.

clue.text: Convey wheels expected at the same time?

indicators.note: wheeling round turns the letters to run backwards

parts.note: ETA is the estimated time of arrival, when someone is expected
idem is Latin for the same

explanation.surface: A driver delivers wheels on the promised arrival time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wheels' looks like a car; it turns ETA IDEM backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass something on, as a medium transmits a message, is a sense of convey.

clue.text: Jumped-up sect member with no leader and no identity

indicators.note: in a down answer, jumping up reads the letters from bottom to top
the first letter is dropped

parts.note: an Essene belonged to an ancient Jewish sect
taken as written

explanation.surface: An upstart cultist has lost their leader and their sense of self.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no leader' drops the first E of ESSENE, leaving SSENE; add NO, and 'Jumped-up' reverses the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Being one and the same, sameness, is a meaning of identity.

clue.text: Queen Elizabeth I royally adopted vessel

indicators.note: the queen's letters take in the next part

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, the Queen's cipher
a monarch speaking of herself says we, the royal plural

explanation.surface: The first Elizabethan queen took over a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elizabeth I' looks like the Tudor monarch; the 'I' goes with 'royally' to make WE.
explanation.definitionFit: A large jug with a wide mouth, a container for water.

clue.text: Series of bi-singles? 'Biblical' woman's all over poor Glenn

indicators.note: her letters spread all over, round the next part

parts.note: Ruth is a woman in the Bible who gives her name to a book, so Ruth's

indicators.note: a poor version is a mangled one, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman from Scripture smothers a hapless man called Glenn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges GLENN to NLENG, which RUTHS goes 'all over'. The definition is computing: binary digits (bits) repeating.
explanation.definitionFit: In data compression, consecutive identical bits are stored as a count, the sequences called this.

clue.text: Born/died out of necessity

indicators.note: the letter is taken out from the following word

parts.note: a need is a necessity
D is the abbreviation for died in records

explanation.surface: A notice of someone born and died through sheer necessity.
explanation.definitionFit: Placed before a married woman's maiden name, the French word means born as.

clue.text: A challenge for Cretan climbers, they say, getting down from it?

indicators.note: signals a word that sounds like one heard

parts.note: eiderdown is the soft down taken from the eider duck

explanation.surface: A tricky climb in Crete, they say, getting off it?
explanation.walkthrough: In a British accent the duck's name loses its final R.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Ida is the highest peak on Crete, a summit for mountaineers there.

clue.text: A beast that's been reduced — to tears, apparently?

definitions.text: A beast that's been reduced — to tears, apparently?

parts.words: A beast that's been reduced — to tears, apparently?
parts.note: a large river reptile's name cut short; that reptile's weeping is proverbially insincere, only apparent

explanation.surface: An animal made to weep, or so it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' looks like 'reduced to tears' but means the name is shortened; the reptile's tears are proverbially false.
explanation.definitionFit: A clipped informal name for the big toothy reptile famous for shedding fake tears.

clue.text: A feature of Boxing Day, going Greek dancing

indicators.note: letters dancing move about into a new order

explanation.surface: A Boxing Day highlight: everyone dancing Greek-style.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxing Day is 26 December, a UK holiday; the King George VI Chase is a horse race at Kempton run that day.
explanation.definitionFit: The King George VI Chase is the big steeplechase of the 26 December racing card.

clue.text: Gallantry award discovered on a new chap from the Agency …

indicators.note: its first letter, the cover, is taken off

parts.note: the QGM is the Queen's Gallantry Medal

explanation.surface: A medal turned up on a newcomer from the security service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discovered' strips the Q from QGM.
explanation.definitionFit: Government man, American slang for an FBI agent, someone from a federal agency.

clue.text: … Frank, mentioned in despatches, offering resistance

definitions.meaning: On His Majesty's Service, printed on official letters in place of a stamp, a frank

explanation.surface: A soldier called Frank, praised in despatches for his resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a name; it is a postal mark on government mail.
explanation.definitionFit: The SI unit measuring electrical resistance, plural; and an abbreviation franked on crown mail.

clue.text: All but mainstream ads broadcast by America?

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters the letters into a new order

explanation.surface: Nearly every mainstream advert goes out on American networks.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the first two words; 'broadcast' rearranges MAINSTREAM ADS, after A.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial British phrase meaning very nearly, almost, the same as 'all but'.
